Yes, `std::string myString;` does call the default constructor in C++11 (and in all versions of C++).

This declaration creates a string object using the default constructor, which initializes `myString` to an empty string (equivalent to `""`).

This is functionally equivalent to:
```cpp
std::string myString{};        // C++11 uniform initialization
std::string myString("");      // Explicit empty string
std::string myString = "";      // Copy initialization with empty string
```

All of these create an empty string with:
- Size/length of 0
- No allocated characters (though small string optimization may reserve some space)
- `myString.empty()` returns `true`
- `myString.c_str()` returns a pointer to a null terminator

So yes, even though there are no parentheses or braces, the default constructor is indeed called when you declare `std::string myString;`.
